Upgradation of Coastal Highways in Gujarat 
*262. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that though Gujarat has 25 per cent of the country's 
coastline with many ports and all sections of the coastal highway along this coast has not 
been upgraded to National Highway; and 
(b) if so, the time envisaged for this upgradation? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) A length of 1034 kilometer of roads along the coastline in Gujarat has 
already been declared as National Highways. This includes 350 kilometer length of roads 
declared as national Highways in February 2004. The declaration of any road as a 
National Highway depends not only on the consideration that it runs along the coast but on 
several other considerations including traffic needs, inter-se priority on all India basis and 
availability of resources. At present emphasis is being given for development of roads 
already declared as National Highways instead of declaring more roads as National 
Highways.

Application of Advanced Technology in space Activities 
*263. DR. K. MALAISAMY. Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) where do we stand in the application of advanced technology in space activities 
in comparison with the developed/developing countries; 
(b) whether our objective to use space technology as an instrument for socio-
economic development of people has been achieved; 
(c) whether the process of finding out the natural resources like water, forest, 
minerals, other potentialities of every State has been completed; and 
(d) if so, how many States have used such information? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) India ranks today as one amongst the top few countries in the world to have 
effectively utilised the advanced space technologies such as satellite remote sensing and 
communications in various social and developmental applications. 
(b) Yes, Sir. The space technology applications have been integrated in areas of direct 
relevance to the socio-economic development of the people such as, natural 
resources, environment and disaster management. Using Satellite based 
telemedicine and tele-education, health care and educational programmes are taken to 
remote parts of the country. 
(c) and (d) Many National and State level applications projects have been carried out 
using satellite remote sensing & Geographic Information System (GIS) in various States. 
Some of the major efforts carried out are towards identifying prospective zones of 
ground water occurrence; monitoring of the performance of the major irrigated 
command areas; reclamation of saline/alkaline affected soils and wasteland reclamation; 
biennial monitoring of forest cover, assessment of biodiversity; study of prospects for 
mineral bearing zones; mapping and dissemination of potential fishery zones; 
infrastructure development in rural and urban areas; coastal regulation zoning; 
environmental impact assessment etc. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
Besides the above, satellite communication technology has been employed to 
provide 2-way speech circuits, television broadcasting including Direct to Home 
services, telemedicine and tele-education services to remote rural areas. Almost all the 
states in the country have made use of the space technology applications. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, I am very happy indeed to note that we are one 
among the notable nations in the world in the application of advanced technology in 
space. I am fairly and broadly satisfied with the reply given by the hon. Minister, except 
on certain specific areas. 
My first supplementary is this. We are able to obtain information from these 
devices. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether such information or the 
data given are illustrative or exhaustive and, whether they are intensive or only 
superficial. The final part of my supplementary is that there are umpteen no. of other 
devices to make survey and exploration. If so, how do they compare with our remote 
sensing and communication system? 
SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, using Indian remote sensing satellite and 
the communication satellite technology, broadly, the entire country is surveyed on a 
particular scale. After that, detailed surveys are carried out, which are further proved by 
ground surveys. So, this is an ongoing process. In the space technology, particularly the 
remote-sensing technology, we are the one of the most advanced countries in the world. 
And, that technology is used in all societal developments and dimensions. The work is on-
going. Detailed surveys are being done for various aspects in particular States. As I said, the 
entire country has already been mapped on a particular scale. The higher scale mapping is 
being done. But it is an integrated approach with communication capability and ground 
surveys and so on, an all-encompassing work to be done with various Government 
departments. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, in the answer it has been stated that the remote-
sensing technology and communication technology are capable of detecting disaster

SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN: Sir, for disaster management, the remote-sensing 
technology is used for identifying land-risk zones and for timely information about floods, 
etc. It is not possible to predict tsunami.

t*265. SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the boys and girls of the North-Eastern States have the 
potential to become a good sportsperson; 
(b) if so, whether there is any scheme under the consideration to establish a sports 
academy in that region with a view to exploit the sports potential; 
(c),if so, the details thereof; and (d) if not, the reasons 
therefor?  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 15 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir, there is no doubt that the boys and girls of the North-
Eastern States have the potential to become good sportspersons. 
(b) and (c) The Government of India have a Scheme for giving grants 
to sponsors of State Sports Academies. The main objective of the Scheme is to 
select the best available talent in sports in the age group 10—13 years, as well 
as top performers in State/National competitions in the age group 10—18 
years, and to prepare and groom them over the years for winning medals for the 
country at the international level. 
The Scheme envisages setting up State Sports Academies as a co-
operative venture with joint funding by the Central Government, State 
Government/UT Administration and a Sponsor. The financial assistance to the 
Academy in respect of capita l, non-recurring costs with an upper cap of Rs. 
8.30 crore is to be shared between the Sponsor, the Central Government and the 
State Government in the ratio of 51:25:24. In addition, recurring cost up to Rs. 
17.00 lakh per annum or 25% of actual expenditure, which ever is less, is 
payable for a period of three years by the Government of India. 
Grants under the Scheme can be availed of only by the following 
sponsors: 
(i)         Public/Private Sector Undertakings 
(ii)        Individual sponsors 
(iii)       NGOs 
Grants are released only on the recommendation of the State 
Government/UT Administration. 
A sponsor can apply for setting up a Sports Academy in a State/ UT 
through the State Government/UT Administration accompanied by all 
required documents. The availability of land for the Academy of a minimum 
of 10 acres in an urban area and about 20 acres in rural areas free of cost, will 
be certified by the State Government/UT Administration. 
16 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) Regrettably, so far no viable proposal has been received from any 
sponsor for setting up a State Sports Academy in the North-East Region.

Availability of drinking water in Delhi 
*269. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the minimum requirement of drinking water in Delhi is not being 
fulfilled; 
(b) If so, the details thereof alongwith the per capita availability of water during 
the last one year; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take to provide adequate safe drinking water to 
the residents of Delhi during this summer? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): 
(a) and (b) Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has reported that against the demand of 850 Million 
Gallon per day (MGD), it supplied, during the last one year, on an average, about 675 
MGD drinking water for about 140 lakh population of Delhi which approximately 
works out to 210 litres of per capita per day availability. 
(c) DJB has reported that in order to provide adequate safe drinking water to the 
residents of Delhi this summer, it shall continue to make efforts secure supply of raw 
water from the Tehri Dam for the Sonia Vihar Water Treatment Plant which has been 
completed. The Board is also taking action to recycle waste water at Water 
Treatment Plants at 
30 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Bhagirathi, Chandrawal, Haiderpur and Wazirabad, which is likely to save about 45 
MGD of drinking water. In addition, as a long term measure, Board has undertaken 
construction of a parallel lined channel from Munak to Haiderpur which would save about 
80 MGD of water through reduction in seepage losses. 
The Board also undertakes regular testing of water from raw water stage upto 
consumer end, by lifting samples daily from distribution network, reservoirs, tube-
wells and rainy-wells. To ensure potability of water, testing Kits have also been 
provided to Junior Engineers.

(d) whether Vrindavan, Giriraj, Barsana, Nand Gaon, Kokila Van, etc. located 
in Uttar Pradesh are culturally significant cities; and

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY). (a) to (c) A scheme for 'Rejuvenation of Culturally Significant Cities' was 
conceived in March, 2000 and draft guidelines were also prepared. However, the 
Scheme was dropped in March, 2005 in view of the proposal of National Urban 
Renewal Mission (NURM). Infrastructure development of Culturally significant cities 
can now be taken up under the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission 
(JNNURM) and Urban Infrastructure Development Scheme for Small and Medium 
Towns (UIDSSMT), launched on 3rd December, 2005. 
(d) As ascertained from Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), there is no policy

development of cities including those culturally significant.

Mauda Thermal Power Plant in Nagpur 
*275. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the steps that have been taken and progress so far been made for 
implementation of the 1000 MW coal-based Mauda Thermal Power Plant in 
Nagpur; 
(b) the expenditure so far incurred th ereon and by when the same is 
likely to be completed; and 
(c) whether any specific difficulties are being faced presently in this 
project? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
to (c) In the course of identificati on of power projects for NTPC's capacity 
addition programme, a site near Mauda was identified as one of the prospective 
sites in Nagpur district of Maharashtra. The works for various site-specific 
studies such as Topographical Survey, Geo-Technical Investigation, Seismic 
Study, Environmental Impact Assessment Study and Make-up Water Study 
etc., for the project were taken up by NTPC to examine the Techno-economic 
viability of the project. So far, approximately Rs. 25 lakhs have been spent by 
NTPC in order to prepare the Feasibility Report and establish techno-economic 
viability of the project. 
42 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The site was identified considering its proximity to Coal Mines of 
Western Coalfields Ltd. about 150 kms away. However, the mines identified 
for supply of coal to the project in Wardha Valley Coal Fields were found to 
be of very small capacities and scattered over a large area. Therefore, linkage 
of coal for the project was granted from lb Valley of Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. 
(MCL) in Orissa, located about 600 Kms away. Consequently, the cost of coal 
transportation works out to be about Rs. 585 per tonne, resulting increase of the 
cost of power by about 45 Paise/Kwh. Thus, economic ranking of Mauda 
Thermal Power Project did not compare favourably with NTPC's proposed pit-
head based integrated Mega power project in Raigarh district of Chhattisgarh 
with a capacity of 4000 MW of meeting the power requirement of the Western 
Region beneficiaries including Maharashtra. 
However, due to acute shortage of power in Western Region in general 
and Maharashtra in particular, the Ministry of Power held detailed discussions 
with NTPC and it has been decided that NTPC would revisit the issue. The 
Ministry of Power shall take up with Ministry of Coal to provide coal linkage 
from Western Coal Fields or from the nearest coal mines. NTPC would also 
examine the feasibility of setting up of Mauda Power Project using coal from lb 
valley and discuss with the beneficiary states, which would be willing to buy 
power at the rate at which this project will be able to offer.

f1793. SHRI PYARELAL KH ANDELWAL: Will the PRIME

58

(c) the specific problem to accord recognition to Hindi in United Nations 
Organization; and 
(d) the number of languages in the world which enjoy recognition in the United 
Nations Organization? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ANAND SHARMA): (a) to (d) The introduction of Hindi as one of the official 
languages of the United Nations has been raised in the World Hindi Conferences and other 
fora time and again. A high level Committee under the chairmanship of External 
Affairs Minister was constituted on 26th February, 2003 followed by a sub-Committee 
under the chairmanship of Minister of State for External Affairs in August, 2003 and a 
core-group headed by the Additional Secretary (Administration) in the Ministry of External 
Affairs in September, 2003 to look into this matter and prepare a road map for realizing 
the objective. As a step in this direction it was decided to prepare an Advocacy Paper 
to present the Indian case with regard to introducing Hindi in the UN. The draft Advocacy 
Paper has been prepared. However, this has implications, both financial and procedural as 
well as legal. The procedure for getting any language recognized as one of the Official 
Languages of the UN involves obtaining approval of the General Assembly to amend 
Rule-51 of the Rules of Procedure. Such a proposal has to be approved by more than half 
of the members of the General Assembly where every member-State has a vote. At 
present the proposal would require approval of 96 member-States given the current 
membership of 191. In addition, recognizing any language as the official language of the 
UN entails substantial increase in the expenditure of the UN wherefore every member 
country has to enhance its contribution, which is why most of the members remain 
passive to support such a proposal. 
At present UN has six Official Languages, which are English, French, Spanish, 
Russian, Chinese and Arabic.

Boundary Issue with China 
1810. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the developments that took for the last two years on boundary issue 
with China; 
(b) where do the talks stand now; and 
(c) whether there's a solution expected? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) and (b) In June 2003, India and China 
each appointed a Special Representative on the boundary question to explore the 
framework of a boundary settlement, proceeding from the political perspective 
of the overall bilateral relationship. There have been six meetings of the Special 
Representatives so far. Based on the first five rounds of talks between the Special 
Representatives, both sides signed the "Agreement on Political Parameters and 
Guiding Principles for Settlement of India-China Boundary Question" on April 
11, 2005 during the visit of the Chinese Premier, HE. Mr. Wen Jiabao to India. 
The sixth round of talks between the Special Representatives was held in 
Beijing from September 26 to September 28,2005, which marked the beginning 
of the second phase of negotiations. In the second phase of negotiations, the two 
Special Representatives are mandated to work out an agreed framework for a 
boundary settlement on the basis of the aforementioned Agreement. Such an 
agreed framework will provide the basis for the delineation and demarcation 
of the India-China boundary to be subsequently undertaken by civil and 
military officials and surveyors of the two sides. 
74 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
In addition, the India-China Joint Working Group on the boundary 
question, which is engaged in tasks re lating to clarification and confirmation 
of the line of actual control and establishment of confidence building measures 
in the India-China border areas, continues its discussions. 
(c) No timeframe has been fixed for the final settlement of the 
boundary question. Both India and China have expressed the conviction that an 
early settlement of the boundary question will advance the basic interests of the 
two countries and should, therefore, be pursued as a strategic objective.

Development of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
1828. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SA NGHI: Will the Minister of 
PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any new method have been proposed in the last five years 
to further develop Panchayati Raj Institution; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AlYAR): (a) to (c) Prior to the setting up of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, the 
Ministry of Rural Development was th e nodal Ministry for Panchayati Raj 
Institutions. A Conference of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj was held on 
11th July 2001 at New Delhi to discuss the measures to be taken to devolve 
functions and powers in accordance with the provisions of the 
88 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Constitution. In pursuance of the Resolution of the Conference, the Ministry of Rural 
Development constituted a Task Force on devolution of Powers and functions to 
Panchayati Raj Institutions. The Task Force submitted its report on 31.8.2001, which 
was sent to all States for their consideration. 
An empowered Sub-Committee on Financial and Administrative Empowerment 
of Panchayati Raj Institutions under the Chairmanship of Minister for Rural Development 
was set up in March 2003 by Planning Commission, in pursuance of a decision 
taken in the National Development Council. The Terms of Reference of the Sub-
Committee include, inter-alia, working out the modalities for strengthening the financial 
domain of the PRIs through transfer of resources from the Centre and State 
Governments, assessing the capacity of the PRIs to raise revenues and other resources and 
to develop an action plan in this regard and analyzing the capability of PRIs at different 
levels to absorb the financial allocation made to the PRIs under different schemes and to 
develop a framework to ensure fiscal discipline and financial accountability at 
different levels of PRIs. The Empowered Sub-Committee has held two meetings so far. 
The last meeting was held on 7th August 2003. The Empowered Sub-Committee has 
been reconstituted on 14.9.2005 with the Union Minister of Panchayati Raj as the 
Chairperson and the Minister of Rural Development as a member of the sub-Committee. 
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj was set up on 27 May 2004. After the Ministry 
was set up, a Conference of Chief Ministers and State Ministers in charge of Rural 
Development and Panchayati Raj on "Poverty Alleviation and Rural Prosperity through 
Panchayati Raj" was organized at New Delhi on 29-30 June 2004, jointly by the 
Ministry of Rural Development and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. The Conference 
was inaugurated by the Prime Minister. Issues relating to effective 
implementation of Part IX and IX A of the Constitution on Panchayati Raj were tabled as 
agenda for discussions by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. These issues included 
effective devolution of functions, finances, functionaries, planning, Gram Sabhas, 
women, reservation for SCs/STs, special problem of SCs/STs, elections, audit, parallel 
bodies, capacity building and training, and state of the Panchayat Report and jurisprudence. 
The Conference decided to hold seven Round Table Conferences to formulate a 
draft action plan towards achiving the objective of 
89 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
strengthening of Panchayati Raj Institutions to enable them to emerge as institutions of 
self-government for the planning and implementation of programmes of economic 
development and social justice as envisioned in the Constitution. Between July-
December, 2004 Ministry of Panchayati Raj convened seven Round Table Meetings 
with the State Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj and evolved by consensus a set of 
ground 150 points for action which have been put together in a compendium that was 
adopted unanimously at the conclusion of the last Round Table in Jaipur. 
A Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj under the Chairmanship 
of the Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been constituted to review the 
implementation of the recommendations. The first meeting of the Council was held 
on 5th-6th August 2005 at Kochi, Kerala. A Committee of Chief Secretaries of States 
and State Panchayati Raj Secretaries has also been constituted under the 
Chairmanship of the Union Secretary (Panchayati Raj) to monitor the progress on 
the implementation of the 150 recommendations of the Seven Round Tables and the 
decisions of the Council of States Ministers of Panchayati Raj. Four review meetings 
of the Committee have so far been held in April 2005, June, 2005, September, 
2005, and November 2005. 
With a view to interacting with Panchayats and carrying out a review with the 
authorities concerned of the progress in implementing the points for action mutually 
agreed to in the Round Tables, a process of visiting the States and UTs at the level of 
Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been initiated. Eight States and two Union 
Territories have been covered so far. These include Karnataka, West Bengal, 
Uttaranchal, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, Or issa, Arunachal Pradesh, Rajasthan, 
Lakshadweep and Chandigarh. Each visit is concluded with a Statement of 
Conclusions jointly signed with the Chief Minister of the State concerned, laying out 
the points of action on which the State would move to operationalise the 
recommendations of the Round Tables. 
An exercise is underway to review different statues with a view to harmonise 
them with the provisions of Part IX of the Constitution. Similarly, the guidelines of 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes are being reviewed to ensure the centrality of 
Panchayats in planning and implementation. As regards new Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes, it is proposed to provide for a central role for Panchayats wherever relevant. 
Thus, for example, the 
90 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
National Rural Employment Guarantee Act provides for the Panchayats to be the 
"principal authorities" for the planning and implementation, of schemes under the Act. 
Steps are also being taken to fill in critical gaps in infrastructure and capacity so that 
Panchayats can effectively fulfill their constitutional role.

Rural business hub scheme 
1830. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI RAJ be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to start 'Rural Business Hub Scheme' in 
the Panchayats of the country; 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, whether Government would consider this in Panchayat 
development programme in future; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. In accordance with the directions indicated by the Prime 
Minister in his address to the Chief Ministers' Conference on "Poverty Eradication and 
Rural Prosperity through panchayati Raj" in June 2004, the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, 
the Ministry of Commerce and the Confederation of Indian Industries (Cll) are working 
together to facilitate building linkages between Panchayats, on the one hand, and 
business enterprises in the public and private sectors, on the other, to create Rural 
Business Hubs in different blocks of the country. The successful Thai experience of 
One Tambon One Product (OTOP), and the Chinese experience of Town and 
Village Enterprises (TVE) are among the models being kept in mind, adapted to Indian 
conditions. Rural Business Hubs are designed to be a Public-Private Panchayat 
Partnership to produce/ improve/refihe goods from locally available resources to 
enable larger market access. A Joint RBH Council, comprising representatives of the 
Government and Cll and eminent individuals working in this area, has been 
constituted for monitoring the process and reviewing the action. 
The Union Government, with the help of State Governments, Panchayats, 
Cll and other similar organizations, has identified 846 potential products and the 
blocks in which these will be promoted on the basis of Memoranda of Understanding 
between key stake holders for ensuring development of the RBH in a set time frame, 
covering every facet of product development, ensuring quality, value addition, market 
access and securing better prices. 
Under the RBH initiative, 30 MOUs have so far been signed between Panchayats 
and Corporate in the public and private sectors. Details are enclosed as Statement 
(See below). 
Cll and Ministry of Panchayati Raj are jointly organizing RBH awareness 
programmes through seminars/conferences at the regional level.

Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) and Central Finance Commission Grants. SGRY is 
implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development. The main objective of the Scheme 
is to provide additional wage employment in the rural areas as also food security, alongside 
the 
96

SGRY is implemented through Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) at District, Block

recommendations of the seven Round Tables of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj 
and to empower Panchayats as institutions of local self-government in accordance with 
the letter and spirit of Article 243G of the Constitution. 
This is a new scheme. Drawal of funds from the Scheme will be entirely based 
on the pace of reform of Panchayati Raj in States. To start with, a Budget provision of 
Rs. 5 crore has been made in the current financial year (2005-06) out of the savings 
from the existing schemes of Ministry of Panchayati Raj. Milestones for reform will 
be identified, benchmarks standardized and releases will be made in accordance with

Health and Welfare of Child 
1841. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: SHRI 
VIJAYJ.DARDA SHRI SANTOSH 
BAGRODIA 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per experts who deliberated at the two day National Consultation 
on Priorities for Children recently organized by the Planning Commission and UNICEF, 
the child health and welfare scenario is dismal, with the country nowhere dose to 
achieving the targets set in the Tenth Five Year Plan; and 
(b) if so, what strategy Government propose to evolve to remedy the situation 
in the remaining period of the Tenth Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) No Sir. In the National 
Consultation on "Priorities of Children in the Eleventh Plan" organized jointly by the 
Planning Commission and United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) with the 
support of Institute of Human Development (IHD), New Delhi, on January 18-
19, 2006, the experts expressed their concern regarding slow progress in 
achieving seme of the goals for children. It may be mentioned that the Consultation 
held was basically to get inputs for the Working Group on Children for the 11th Five 
Year Plan. 
It may further be mentioned that it would not be entirely appropriate to say that in 
regard to the Tenth Plan Targets for health and welfare of children, the scenario has 
been dismal. The recently completed Mid Term Appraisal (MTA) of the Tenth Plan 
shows that there has been good progress in achieving some monitorable goats for 
children. There is reduction in the number of out of school children from 42 million at 
the beginning of plan period to 8.1 milllion in September 2004 as a result of 
enrolment drive launched during the second year of Tenrn Plan. Similarly, gender gap in 
literacy, which started narrowing in the 90s La. by coming 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
down to 21.59% in 2001 from 24.85% in 1991, is expected to narrow down 
further by the end of the Tenth Plan. The total literacy rate has also improved 
significantly from 52.21 % in 1991 to 64.84% in 2001 and it is expected to 
achieve the Tenth Plan target of literacy rate of 75% by 2007. The Infant 
Mortality Rate (IMR) has also been on the decline i.e. from 72 per 1000 births 
in 1998 to 60 in 2003 and is expected to decline further.

Growth parameters of Maharashtra 
1845. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Planning Commission has recently examined all 
growth parameters of Maharashtra State; 
(b) if so, the observations on the basis of these parameters in respect of that State; 
and 
(c) whether it is a fact that Maharashtra has been described as an example of a 
failed State; if so, the basis therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) The annual average Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) growth target 
assigned to Maharashtra during the Tenth Plan is 7.43 per cent. The State has recorded 
annual average GSDP growth rate of over 7% during the first four years of the Tenth Plan 
and is all set to achieve the targeted overall growth rate, though there may be set back in 
respect of agricultural growth rate. However, the State needs to address problems relating to 
stagnant agriculture, watershed development, incomplete irrigation projects and 
increasing regional imbalances. 
(c) No, Sir. However, during the Annual Plan 2006-07 discussions with the State 
Government, it was pointed out that the State had not provided balanced development 
in all the regions of the State.   . 
BPL people in Andhra Pradesh 
1846. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of people living below poverty line in Andhra Pradesh as 
per NSSO 2000; 
(b) the percentage of people living below poverty line in Andhra Pradesh as 
on date; and 
(c) whether Government have any specific concrete action plan to eradicate 
poverty from the State within a specific time period? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN):(a) and (b) The Planning Commission 
116 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
estimates the incidence of poverty at national and state level from the large scale 
sample survey on household consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample 
Survey Organisation (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years. The latest 
available data from such survey is from NSS 55th Round, which was conducted during 
1999-2000. According to the result of that survey, the percentage of persons living 
below the poverty line in Andhra Pradesh is 15.77. 
(c) In the Tenth Plan (2002-07) the Planning Commission has set a monitorable 
target for reduction of poverty by 5% points by 2007 and accordingly, the Government 
has taken concrete action to reduce poverty in the country as a whole, including the State 
of Andhra Pradesh. 
In rural areas, the programmes which are being implemented by the Ministry 
of Rural Development for upliftment of BPL families are (i) Sampoorna Grameen 
Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), (ii) Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), (iii) 
Indira Awas Yojana (IAY), (iv) National Food for Works Programme (NFFWP) and 
(v) National Rural Employment Guarantee Act. 
The poverty alleviation programme which is being implemented in urban areas 
is Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY). This programme seeks to provide 
gainful employment to the urban unemployed or underemployed poor through setting up of 
micro enterprises and also through provision of Wage Employment by utilizing their 
labour for construction of useful public assets. There is another programme called 
'Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana' (VAMBAY) and National Slum 
Development Programme (NSDP) which are being implemented to provide 
shelter for urban slum dwellers. 
The Public Distribution System in India has been more focused and targeted 
towards the very poor category. The "Antyodaya Anna Yojana" provides 35 kgs of 
foodgrains to the poorest of the poor families at a highly subsidized rate of Rs. 2 per 
kg., for wheat and Rs. 3 per kg., for rice. Recently, the coverage of Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana has been expanded from 2.0 crore (BPL) families to 2.5 crore families in 
2005. The State Governments have been advised to give priority to the 
households from the poorest and the backward blocks and/or where nutritional 
deficiency is more widespread, while identifying the beneficiaries.

Energy Coordination Committee 
1852. SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRlGIREDDY: SHRI K. 
RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a meeting of the Energy Coordination 
Committee has been held to find ways of feeding country's growing hunger for fuel; 
(b) whether it is a fact that there is a shortage of 38 per cent of natural gas and 
7 per cent of coal supplies in generation of power; 
(c) if so, in what manner Government are thinking of meeting the demand; 
(d) whether Government are in the process of approving production of coal from 
ten more mines; and 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. A meeting of the Energy Coordination Committee under the Chairmanship 
of Prime Minister was held on 10.2.2006. 
(b) During 2005-06 (Upto January, 2006), against a requirement of gas (at 
90% Plant Load Factor) of 57.52 Million Metric Standard Cubic Meters Per Day 
(MMSCMPD), the actual supply has been 35.87 MMSCMPD, thus leaving a 
gap of 37.6%. Similarly, against a projected demand of coal of 310 million tons for 
2005-06, Ministry of Coal agreed to supply 298 million tons from indigenous sources. 
Assuming a transit loss of 6 Metric Tons, the shortfall was 18 Million Tons (5.8%). 
(c) Steps have been taken to increase availability of gas from domestic 
sources by awarding gas blocks for exploration and production activities in various 
sedimentary basins of the country under New Exploration Licensing Policy and 
also to import of gas in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas. To bridge the gap between 
demand and supply of coal during 2005-06, import of 13.45 million tons of coal has been 
decided during 2005-06. As a long term measure, new coal blocks are being 
allocated by the Ministry of Coal to power producers/utilities for captive mining to 
meet requirement of their power plants. 
(d) and (e) For meeting the coal demand, Coal India Limited has identified 
100 projects to be taken up during Tenth Five Year Plan period. The total capacity of 
these projects is 250.75 million tons. Out of these, 65 projects with aggregate 113.265 
million tons have been sanctioned so far. 15 projects are to be approved by Coal India 
Limited under the powers delegated to them. Out of 20 projects to be approved by the 
Government 6 have been recommended by the Public Investment Board. It is envisaged 
that the projects taken up during the Tenth Five Year Plan would contribute 82.24 million 
tons during the terminal year of X Plan i.e. 2006-07.

R.K. ANAND: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that vast majority of rural population still has no access to 
electricity and is dependent on kerosene lamps and lanterns; 
(b) if so, the schemes formulated for electrification of 25000 remote 
villages/hamlets; 
(c) the reasons for not electrifying a single remote village of Bihar under remote 
village electrification programme as on 30.11.2004; 
(d) the list of 273 remote villages of Bihar identified for electrification under 
remote village electrification programme, district-wise; and 
137

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) Yes, Sir. 
As per 2001 census there are about 78 crore rural households in the country having 
no access to electricity.

where grid connectivity is either not feasible or not cost effective. The Ministry of 
Non-Conventional Energy Sources (MNES) is implementing the Remote Village 
Electrification Programme for electrification of such remote un-electrified villages 
numbering 25,000 through non-conventional energy sources.

Rural Electrification in Assam 
1863. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of electrified villages and households in the North-Eastern State, 
especially in Assam; 
(b) the reasons for poor rate of growth in electrifying the villages and 
households; and 
(c) the target year, if any, for completion of 100 per cent village and households 
electrification as envisioned in the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) Village 
electrification level in the eight North-Eastern States was 73.32% as on 31.3.2005. As 
regards, level of households electrification, these States have reported electrification of 
24.26% as on 31.3.2004. The level of village electrification and households electrification 
in Assam was 75.95% and 16.54% respectively as per 2001 Census. The State-wise 
status of village electrification and households electrification in these eight North-Eastern 
States is given in the enclosed Statement-I (See below). 
(b) The pace of village and households  electrification in these States 
has been slow mainly because of: 
(i) State Power Utilities were reluctant to take up rural electrification, as it is non 
remunerative and leads to more losses. 
(ii) State Power utilities were in bad financial health and were unable to provide 
support to the schemes. 
(iii) The State Power Utilities did not have adequate man-power in rural areas for 
maintenance of rural electricity infrastructure sc created. 
(iv) Funds did not reach the implementing agencies in time. 
(v) The pace and direction of rural electrification was left to the states which had a 
decelerating effect on rural electrification. 
(c) Under Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY) 
100% electrification of villages and access to electricity to all rural 
households is intended to be completed by 2009.

1882. DR. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

SIBAL):(a)Yes Sir. 
(b) to (d) Government is setting up an Early Warning System for Tsunami and 
Storm Surges covering the entire Indian coastline with the following components: 
strengthening of the existing seismological network to indicate, near real time 
occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes; 
installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean bottom at appropriate 
locales in the Indian Ocean, with real tim connectivity; 
Tide gauge and data buoys networking to validate arrival of tsunami

Modelling of the inundation scenarios for the entire coast and mapping of

collection of information, analysis and generating status advisories.

be operational by September, 2007

Andhra Pradesh and Orissa for locating Tsunami Warning System in these states. The 
decision to locate the Tsunami Early Warning Centre at the Indian National Centre for 
Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad was taken with a view to make 
optimal utilization of the facilities created at INCOIS for Satellite Oceanography and 
Statellite Communication etc. INCOIS is the agency of the Ministry of Ocean

Area vulnerable to natural disaster 
1883. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: 
SHRI SURESH BHARDWAJ: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 54% of India's area is vulnerable to earthquakes; 
(b) the percentage of Orissa's land area vulnerable to earthquake, cyclonic 
winds and flood damage; and 
(c) the steps government are taking for early alarming system for this and to 
strengthening the vulnerable houses which face highest risk of damage? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As per the seismic zoning map published by Bureau of Indian Standards 
(BIS) the country has been divided into four zones. Zone-V is considered to be most 
seismically active while the zone-ll is the least. As per this map 16% of Orissa's land area 
falls in seismic zone-Ill and 84% falls in zone-ll which are considered to be moderate 
and low intensity zones, respectively. The whole of Orissa State is also vulnerable to 
cyclones, characterized by strong winds; very heavy and intense rain fall causing floods. 
In particular, the coastal districts are also very much vulnerable to storm surges 
associated with cyclones. 
(c) At present there is no early alarming system for earthquakes, as there is no 
scientific technique available, the world over, which can forecast earthquakes in terms of size, 
space and time. However, BIS has published a number of guidelines for construction, repair 
and seismic strengthening of buildings. Adherence to these guidelines would definitely 
minimize the damage to the property and loss of lives. 
India Meteorological Department also has a well established and time tested 
system for monitoring and forecasting of intensity and movement of tropical 
cyclones. A network of Cyclone Detection Radars has also been installed alongwith the 
east and west coast.

1887. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether at present there is no policy on dredging; 
(b) whether investments in dredging is minimal; 
(c) whether Government have any proposal to formulate a national policy 
on dredging; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (e) Government has already 
formulated a dredging policy after detailed discussions with all the stake 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
holders, Salient features of this policy adopted with effect from 1st April 2004 for a 
period of three years; are: 
(i) The maintenance dredging requirement of Kolkata Port shall continue to be 
met by Dredging Corporation of India Limited (DCI). 
(ii) All major ports other then Kolkata Port shall float open tenders for their 
dredging contracts. 
- (iii) DCI shall have the right of first refusal if its bid is within 10% of lowest 
technically qualified offer, for both maintenance dredging and capital 
dredging works including the capital dredging requirements of Kolkata 
Port. 
(iv) To ensure level playing field between the DCI and other Indian dredging 
companies, the right of first refusal has been allowed to all Indian companies 
provided their bid is within 10% of the lowest offer. If more than one Indian 
company including DCI participate in the tender, right of first refusal will go 
to that Indian Company which has quoted the lowest and is within 10% of lowest 
technically qualified offer.

adequate dredging capacity to meet the increasing requirements of Ports, it also

Modifying MPLAD Scheme 
1900. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA: Will the Minister of 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering a proposal to abrogate or replace or

(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI G.K. VASAN): (a) and (b) 
There is no proposal to abrogate the Member of Parliament Local Area 
Development Scheme (MPLADS) under consideration. However, MPLADS 
Guidelines have been comprehensively revised and issued on 16.11.2005. The salient 
features of the revised Guidelines are given at enclosed Statement (See below). The 
Ministry has further sought views of all Members of Parliament, State Governments 
and the concerned Central Ministries/Departments for improvement in the 
implementation of the Scheme. 
Statement 
Salient Features of Revised Guidelines of MPLADS 
Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) is under 
implementation since 1993-94. The Guidelines under the Scheme were revised from 
time to time and lastly it was revised in April, 2002. Subsequently, certain 
clarificatory circulars have been issued. Now, a 
196 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
comprehensive revision have been made and a fresh set of Guidelines has been issued 
on 16th November, 2005. These Guidelines are based on the feed back received 
from Hon'ble MPs, the suggestions of the Committees on MPLADS (Lok Sabha and 
Rajya Sabha), the observations made by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and 
the operational experience gained in the monitoring of the Scheme. 
In the revised Guidelines, some of the improvements are as under: 
(i) Important sectors like drinking water, education, public health, sanitation 
and roads have been given priority. 
(ii) Earmarking of funds to the extent of 15% and 7.5% funds for the development 
of SC and ST inhabited areas respectively. 
(iii) Automatic release of Rs. 1 crore in respect of MPs at the time of constitution 
of Lok Sabha and election to Rajya Sabha without fulfillment of conditions 
including monthly progress report. 
(iv) Automatic release of first instalment in any financial year in those cases where 
two instalments have been released in the previous year. 
(v) The role of Implementing Agen cies, District Authority, State 
Government and Central Government have been clearly delineated. 
(vi) Limit of Rs. 25 lakh of individual work has been removed while maintaining 
the same for Trusts/Societies/NGOs. 
(vii) List of the permissible items have been removed. Instead the list of works 
prohibited under MPLADS has been given. 
(viii) MPLADS works costing upto Rs. 10 lakh for natural calamities like floods, 
cyclone etc. by MPs from the non-affected areas of their State. 
(ix) The maximum limit for rehabilitation of work in the affected areas by severe 
calamities have been raised to Rs. 50 lakh. 
(x) A time frame for all the works completed from 1993-94 onwards has been 
prescribed for submission of Utilization Certificates and Audit 
Certificates. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
(xi) Utilization Certificate the previous financial year and the Audit 
certificate for the funds utilized in the year prior to the previous year 
have also been made the pre-requisites for the release of the second 
instalment in a year. 
(xii) The role of Panchayati Raj In stitutions and Urban and Local bodies 
as Implementing Agencies has been stressed. 
Statistical system in the country 
1901. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that statistical system in the country is still 
outdated and as a result the various statistics prepared by Union Government 
and its agencies fall short of accuracy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
 
(c) the steps being taken/proposed to be taken to modernize statistical 
system In the country; and 
(d) the results achieved/proposed to be achieved thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI G.K. VASAN): (a) and 
(b) No Sir. In general statistics gene rated by the statistical system in the 
country are based on scientific methodologies and correctly reflect the 
situation in the country. However, in view of evolving new methodologies or 
advancement in technologies/statistical techniques, there is always scope for 
improvement in the statistical system. 
(c) Major steps taken by the Government to modernize the statistical system 
in the country are as follows: 
(i) Setting-up of a National Statistical Commission, 
(ii) Implementation of World Bank assisted project, namely, India 
Statistical Strengthening Project, 
(iii) Setting-up of a Central Institute for training in official statistics, 
(iv) Setting-up of a data warehouse of official statistics, and 
(v) Introduction of advance techniques for data processing. 
198 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The expected achievements of these steps are: 
(i) Constitution of the National Statistical Commission is expected to provide an 
effective and adequately empowered coordination mechanism for statistical 
activities in the country and to evolve national policies and priorities relating 
to the statistical system. 
(ii) Successful completion of the implementation of the India Statistical 
Strengthening Project is expected to  result in contributions towards 
strengthening of the State statistical system, establishment of strong communication 
links among various units of the statistical system, creation of a National Business 
Register to facilitate periodical surveys of business/economic units, 
improvement in the availability and quality of service sector statistics and 
better utilization of survey capabilities available in the private sector. 
(iii) Setting-up of a Central Institute for training of official statistics will help in 
skill development of the persons dealing with official statistics in Central 
and State Governments.

1924. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to State: 
(a) the percentage of people living below poverty line in India and the State of 
Rajasthan (urban and rural break-up); 
(b) the percentage of families who have so far been assisted under SJSRY;  
(c) the number of such families who could actually be brought above poverty level; 
 
(d) whether Government have launched any new schemes for poverty 
alleviation in urban areas; 
(e) if so, the salient features thereof including the amount allocated and utilized, 
scheme-wise: 
(f) whether any achievements were made under the new schemes; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof, particularly with reference to Rajasthan? 
220 

[9 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI AJAY MAKEN): (a) As per the estimates of 
Planning Commission in 1999-2000, at All India level 26.1% of the 
population (27.09% in rural areas and 23.62% in urban areas) was living below 
poverty line. For the State of Rajasthan this estimate was 15.28% (13.74% in 
rural areas and 19.85% in urban areas). 
(b) to (g) With a view to ameliorate the living conditions of the Urban Poor 
and providing employment opportunities to the Urban poor, Ministry of Urban 
Employment & Poverty Alleviation is implementing an employment oriented 
urban poverty alleviation programme named Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar 
Yojana (SJSRY), on all India basis with effect from 1.12.1997. The Scheme is 
funded in proportion of 75:25 between Centre and the States. The SJSRY strives 
to providing gainful employment to the urban unemployed or under-employed poor 
through (i) encouraging the setting up of Self-employment ventures by those who 
have not studied beyond 9th standard and (ii) provision of wage employment by 
utilizing their labour for construction of socially and economically useful public 
assets. 
Since inception of the scheme on 1.12.1997 and as reported upto 
31.12.2005, 7,91,348 micro-enterprises have been set up and 6,71,867 urban 
poor have been provided skill training. Similarly 578.35 lakhs of mandays of 
work have been generated under Wage Employment Component of SJSRY. 
For the current year, 2005-06, Rs. 160 crore has been allocated as Central share 
for the SJSRY and so far (as on 1.3.2006) Rs. 101.90 crore has been released to 
the State/UTs for the implementation of the scheme. 
In the State of Rajasthan, as reported by the State Government through 
Quarterly Progress Reports, 41398 micro enterprises have been set up, 17943 
urban poor have been provided skill training and 22.82 lakhs of mandays of 
work have been generated under the SJSRY.

. Need to tap Natural Resources for Power Generation in Assam 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR (Assam) : Sir, electricity is 
one of the essential commodities for the progress of a State leading to 
socio-economic development, industrial growth depends on electricity. 
Assam is lagging behind in comparison to other States in industrial growth. 
Industrial growth leads to the opening of avenues for employment including 
self-employment.   So, it is imperative that there is quality as well as 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [9 March, 2006] 
uninterrupted power supply. Though the installed capacity in Assam is about 
575 MW, at present the capacity is reduced to 275 MW due to Suspension of 
operations of both BTPS and CTPS owing to high fuel cost. The present 
demand for power in Assam is around 600 MW. So, the State is reeling under 
severe power crisis, even if the existing power stations run with their optimum 
capacities still there will be shortage of  power to cater to the demands of 
Assam. Under these circumstances, ther e is no other alternative than to 
harness the available resources in the geographical area of Assam to 
generate electricity. As far as thermal power is concerned, there is abundant 
quantity of coal in upper Assam, estimated to be around 320 million tonnes 
and it may last more than 100 years with generating capacity of 500 MW of 
power. So far Assam coal has not yet been utilised for power generation 
because of low ash content and high sulphur content. With the sophisticated 
technologies, this type of coal can be us ed for generation of electricity. There 
is a possibility of coal transportation through the River Brahmaputra from 
Dibrugarh to Jogigopa by ships.

Need to widen the scope of AIBP Scheme in Tripura 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura) : Sir, it is appreciable that 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) has been made applicable to 
minor irrigation sector in Tripura from 1999-2000. Under AIBP schemes funds 
are available for lift irrigation and Diversion Schemes in Tripura. But owing to 
certain geographical characteristics, about 2,80,000 hectares of land of 
Tripura cannot be irrigated by either Lift Irrigation or Diversion Schemes as 
these lands do not have the supply of surface water during lean season. The 
farmers largely demand deep tube wells for such lands. As deep tube wells do 
not come under AIBP, funds cannot be arranged for it. Moreover, the present 
scope of AIBP funding norms does not incl ude renovation, special repairs and 
pipeline extension works. So, the norms have to be relaxed for Tripura where 
there are 1178 Lift Irrigation Schemes  and 26 Diversion Schemes. So, I urge 
upon the Government to consider deep tube wells for inclusion in AIBP 
Schemes and to provide at least 15 per cent AIBP fund for renovation, repairs 
and pipeline extension works for the North-Eastern States in general and 
Tripura in particulars.

has also taken care to ensure that PDS kerosene is not diverted for 
adulteration or black marketing. There is  also surveillance by the authorities 
concerned. And, if any deal er found indulging in malpractice, his dealership is

having these many safeguards, the adulteration of petrol and diesel is rampant 
in the State of Andhra Prades h. One of the reasons for this is that in a State

mobile laboratory with the oil companies to cover this entire State which has 
2,75,069 sq. kms. of area. As  a result of this, the existing mobile labs are not

adulteration have become t he order of the day. So, I request the Petroleum

SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, conservation of flora

Act, 2000, and Maharashtra's Act have utte rly failed in controlling the use of 
non-biodegradable bags. The State Govern ments are allowing, on paper, only 
20-micron thickness of plastic bags. But, when one goes to market, one will 
find plastic bags even 100-micron thickness. This is all because there is strong 
'plastic lobbies' in all States whic h are preventing State Governments from 
taking any strict measure.  Even at the Union level,

Mention is pertaining to the problem of gender disparity in education. 
Sir, gender inequality continues to be a formidable problem 
worldwide, especially in the developing countries. It has come to be 
recognised as one of the most significa nt forces that perpetuate poverty, 
besides excluding women from the developmental process. Rightly, promoting 
gender equality and empowering women constitutes one of the highest 
Millennium Development Goals of the UN to which 198 nations are the 
signatories, including India. 
 Women's education's critical to secure gender equality. In our 
neighbourhood, Bangladesh has achieved dramatic increase in the enrolment 
and attendance of girls through elimination of school fees for girls as also by 
providing toilets and safe drinking water in schools. But, in India, no specific 
policy decision concerning free girl-child education has been implemented 
though there have been some tentative effo rts in the past. Provision of toilet 
and safe drinking water is nowhere near reality. Therefore, gender gap persists 
and the difference in the enrolment rates of boys and girls has touched as 
high as nearly six per cent, whereas it is around three per cent in Bangladesh, 
Other related areas of concern include inadequate progress in maternal and 
child mortality rates as well as low levels  of female literacy. It is, therefore, 
imperative to initiate innovative prog rammes for improving girls' education 
which would impact on women's well-being and contribute   to   their   overall   
development   and   empowerment.     Policy

Plight of brick chamber industry and its workers 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to bring to the 
notice of the Government the miserable plight of brick chamber owners and 
workers in the country in general, and of Tamil Nadu in particular, due to the 
high rate of 16 per cent central excise duty imposed on this rural industry. 
There are over 2,000 brick chambers in Tamil Nadu that provides employment 
to more than 50 lakh people, belonging to  the lower strata of the society, 
particularly the Scheduled Castes, the Sc heduled Tribes and the OBCs. In the 
backward and drought-prone district s of Madurai, Ramanathapuram and 
Sivaganga alone, there are about 200 brick chambers providing employment to 
over 25,oop people. The recent hike in the central excise duty to 16 per cent 
has adversely affected the brick industry and has posed imminent danger to 
the livelihood of lakhs of workers in Ta mil Nadu, and millions of them in the 
country. As bricks are the basic requirement  for the infrastructure which has to 
develop fast, this unrealisti c rate of excise duty will slow down infrastructure 
building which will have a direct bearing on our economy. The exemption from 
excise duty given to brick chambers with annual sale up to Rs. 1 crore does 
not help, because the profit  margin is very less since brick chambers employ 
more workers. This is one rural industry which is labour-intensive and employs 
a good number of women. In view of t hese facts, I appeal to the Government 
to drop the excise duty

SHRI E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, many

Eastern countries, but I am still awai ting the reply concerning action taken

system for making arrangements for transportation of corpses of those 
unfortunate Indian labourers and for settling the claims involving the 
companies/employers of the deceased. For this, I think, there should be a

SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI (Nominated ): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, 
empowerment of women is very crucial for building communal harmony. As 
the country is aware, there is a powerful connection between communal 
harmony and empowering of women.  If women are sensitised and 
empowered, they can have a strong in fluence on family members, who might 
have been involved in communal conf licts. Empowerment of women is 
essential for the prevention of communal riots. 
We need to instill confidence  in women and, also, a yearning to use 
their lives well. 
The interplay between women's empowerment and prevention of 
communal riots became clear in 2002 when women volunteers of Hyderabad-
based Confederation of Voluntary Associ ation (COVA) successfully prevented 
eruption of riots in reaction to the si tuation of Gujarat. Ri sking their lives, 
women from various communities came to gether on March 8, 2002,. to form a 
human chain which prevented riots by simply holding laws. This shows the 
strong impression of empowered women. They came together to show that 
they do not want violence. 
Empowering of women is a testimony to the fact that power to 
contain communal violence does not rest with the men only.

contain the incidence of taxation, resource mobilisation, rationalisation and 
simplification of procedures, giving certain reliefs, incentives, etc. These are
